$comment: The families this season grades, chosen by hand. data/pool.json is built from this by npm run apply:curation, which resolves each scenario's leaderboard id against the taxonomy and refuses a name KovaaK's does not publish. It exists because the pool file carries thresholds, sources and sanity readouts alongside the choices, and editing 264 scenario names inside that is not a thing anybody does accurately. This file is only the choices. Static Clicking is absent on purpose: those eleven families were built by hand in the season editor and are carried through untouched.
$rungs: Four per family, easiest first, one per window. A family is one test at four difficulties - not necessarily one author's lineage. Where no single lineage spans the bands the rungs come from whoever cut that difficulty, which is what data/pool.json's $families note already permits and what the Static Clicking families already do: its Micro family runs SCS, Cartoon, Anima and Aimerz+ in four rungs. What each family must hold is the sub-skill and an honest ascent.
$rename: Categories whose families are kept exactly as they are and only the name changes. Clicking becomes Static Clicking because it is now one of two clicking categories. Its families are not curated from this file and are edited in pool.json directly; two have left since the rename, both on measurements rather than taste. Pokeball moved to Speed Switching because its four rungs fire a drill at 22 to 54 shots per kill and cannot be clicking. Vertical was retired because the ClickTrack lineage holds only three cuts above the Expert board floor and four axis families wanted them - Vertical's best was 1,174 entries, nine players deciding rank 16. Nine families now.
$retire: Categories whose families are replaced wholesale, so the old ones are dropped rather than carried. Tracking and Switching are retired because the sub-skill split cuts across them: Smoothbot and PGT are Precise, Ground Plaza is Reactive, and Controlsphere and Raw Control are Control Tracking, which this season does not grade. Leaving them would also put the same scenario in two families.

Dynamic Clicking.$why: Clicking a target that is moving, where the shot has to lead rather than land. Pasu is the canonical bot for it and Voltaic grades three separate Pasu scenarios in one benchmark, so three Pasu-derived families here is that benchmark's own reading of the sub-skill rather than one test counted three times. Ten families rather than eleven: Popcorn MV was the eleventh and came out, because KovaaK's types four of its six cuts as Tracking. A family whose own game calls it a different aim type is one the queue would partition wrongly, whatever the benchmark sheets say.

families.why: Voltaic's own dynamic clicking ladder, on the largest boards in the sub-skill - 230,670 entries at Novice. If one family has to be right, it is this one.

The raspberry-target cut of the same bot: smaller targets, same movement, so it separates target size from the leading. Expert takes 1w4t Pasu Raspberry Grandmaster over VT Pasu Rasp Elite, whose board carries 829.

The original 1wall5targets lineage, which is where dynamic clicking was measured before any benchmark existed and still the most-played of it - 389,281 entries on the reload cut. Slowed, standard, shrunk, then the no-quick-swap variant. pasu nqs reload sat at Expert on a board of 9,541 and is the one cut of this lineage Aimerz+ grades Easy - the Expert rung was the easiest scenario in the family. The four are reordered onto what the sheets grade: the slow and no-quickswap cuts at the bottom, then the canonical 1wall5targets_pasu Reload, then the small-target cut that Aimerz+ and Jade Palace both grade Hard.
Voltaic's reload cuts, which ask the same shot under magazine pressure. A different test from Pasu Classic despite the shared word: these are Voltaic's own four difficulties, authored as a ladder.
Targets that change direction on contact, so the lead has to be re-taken mid-shot. Voltaic and Viscose both grade it and their tiers interleave, which is what fills all four windows here.
Many small targets moving at once, which tests target selection as much as the click. Voltaic's three tiers then rAim's Goated cut, the thinnest of them carrying 7,917 entries.

A target that reverses through 180 degrees, which is the sharpest lead-change in the sub-skill. Voltaic's two cuts then Revosect's two, ascending across the pair. B180 rAim Easy is Revosect's Easy cut and sat at Advanced, above B180 Voltaic, which Voltaic grades Advanced and Jade Palace grades Easy. Two sheets put the standard cut above the easy one and the ladder had them the other way round, so the two are swapped.
Aimerz+'s pipe lineage: targets travelling a fixed path, so the shot is a timing problem rather than a reading one. Four tiers by one author across two seasons of their sheet.
Erratic direction changes with no fixed path, which is the reading end of dynamic clicking rather than the timing end. One author, four cuts.

The angelic bot, which drifts rather than strafes, so the lead is continuous instead of stepped. No single author cut it at four difficulties; psalmTS and Pasu each cut it at two, and the four ascend across them.

Precise Tracking.$why: Holding the crosshair on a target that moves predictably - smoothness rather than reaction. The deepest sub-skill in the corpus: 22 lineages carry two solid rungs and eleven reach four, so this is the one rebuilt category where eleven families was not a compromise.

families.why: Voltaic's smoothness ladder, on the largest board in tracking at 326,600 entries. Expert is Pauer's cut rather than VT Smoothbot Elite, whose board carries 691.
A target on a winding path, so the hand keeps turning instead of settling. Four Voltaic tiers, including the Novice Hard cut that fills the gap to Intermediate.
rungs: VT Snake Track Novice S5 Hard

families.why: Precise ground tracking, Voltaic's own four tiers end to end. The Elite board is 3,674 - thin for this sub-skill, but a ladder one author wrote rather than one assembled here.

The invincible cut of the same test: no kill, so the run never resets and the score is time on target alone. Revosect and Voltaic each cut it twice and the four ascend across them. Its Novice rung was swapped down to an entry cut the sheets band Novice: the bottom of the ladder is meant to be a scenario a beginner can load without being beaten by it, and the difficulty there now comes from the threshold rather than from the test.
A small orb on a smooth path. The 15% Slower cut sits between Novice and Intermediate, which is what lets this family avoid VT PreciseOrb Elite and its board of 273.
Raw control with no strafe pattern to read, which isolates the hand from the head. Viscose's entry cut, then Aimerz+ and Astro's three.

A sphere held at distance, graded by size and range rather than speed - so the four rungs are one test at four target sizes and nothing else moving. The cleanest difficulty axis in the pool. Its Novice rung was swapped down to an entry cut the sheets band Novice: the bottom of the ladder is meant to be a scenario a beginner can load without being beaten by it, and the difficulty there now comes from the threshold rather than from the test.
Viscose's precise lineage: four tiers by one author, on boards from 7,830 to 240,024.

Smoothness on a sphere rather than a bot, which removes the strafe pattern entirely. Viscose's easier cut, the base scenario, then Astro's two. Smoothsphere Diamond sat at Advanced above the standard Smoothsphere. Astro is the only author who grades both and grades Diamond Easy against Smoothsphere Normal, so the two are swapped to the order its own author published. Its Novice rung was swapped down to an entry cut the sheets band Novice: the bottom of the ladder is meant to be a scenario a beginner can load without being beaten by it, and the difficulty there now comes from the threshold rather than from the test.
A glider path - long, shallow direction changes that punish over-correction rather than slow reaction. Opens on Level 1 rather than the 60% Larger cut, which KovaaK's types as Switching.
Aimerz+'s precise lineage, all four rungs from their S1 sheet. Their earlier Normal and Hard cuts are typed Clicking by KovaaK's and are left out for it.

Reactive Tracking.$why: Tracking a target that changes direction unpredictably, so the cost is reaction rather than smoothness. Seven families, not eleven. The corpus holds 19 lineages with two solid rungs and only seven that reach four without borrowing a scenario some sheet files under a different sub-skill; padding it would mean grading reaction on boards of a few hundred people.

families.why: Voltaic's air ladder - a target free in three dimensions, which is the hardest reading in the game. Expert is Air Angelic, the drifting cut.
The same reading held to the floor plane. Four Voltaic tiers, including the Novice Hard cut.
Reactive tracking with cover and depth, so the target leaves the plane. Voltaic's three tiers, then Viscose's thin cut.
Voltaic S5's air scenario, opened on its own Entry cut so the family has a real beginner rung instead of starting at Novice.
rungs: VT Aether Entry S5 Precision Focus

families.why: The celestial air lineage at four speeds, from the slowed no-UFO cut up to Divine. One test, four difficulties, boards from 17,531 to 117,829.
rungs: Air CELESTIAL No UFO Easy Slowed

families.why: Sparky's ground plaza, the most-played reactive scenario outside Voltaic. Easy, the one-way cut, the base scenario, then thin. Ground Plaza Sparky v3 OW sat at Intermediate below the standard V3. Aimerz+ grades OW Hard and Astro grades it Advanced, against Normal and Easy for the plain V3, so the Overwatch cut moves up one and the standard cut down one. Its Novice rung was swapped down to an entry cut the sheets band Novice: the bottom of the ladder is meant to be a scenario a beginner can load without being beaten by it, and the difficulty there now comes from the threshold rather than from the test.
The invincible strafe lineage: no kill, so the target never stops changing direction. Long, fast, thin, then raspberry, which is the order those cuts get harder.

Speed Switching.$why: Moving between static targets as fast as they can be hit. Eight families. This sub-skill has the most candidates of any - 26 lineages with two solid rungs - and the fewest that turn into a ladder: most of the rest are one author's easy-and-hard pair, which is two rungs and cannot be stretched to four honestly.

families.why: Hand-built into Static Clicking over two hours and moved here on a measurement, not a preference. All four rungs fire a Poke-Drill at 22.1, 27.7, 31.8 and 54.4 shots per kill across 119 runs of the corpus; the 191 correctly-labelled clicking scenarios sit between 1.0 and 1.3, so a single click kills nothing here and the family cannot be clicking of any kind. KovaaK's types all sixteen Pokeball scenarios in the corpus as Switching, and the benchmark labels land eight of them on Speed Switching - AimSpeed, Viscose, Avasive and Revosect - against two Lemon calls Stability. The rungs are unchanged from the Static Clicking build.
Voltaic's speed ladder, four tiers, opening on the largest switching board in the game at 348,412 entries. Its Elite board is 933, the thinnest rung in this category.
Small dots at speed, which puts the cost on the stop rather than the travel. Opened on the 30% larger community cut so the beginner rung is easier than Voltaic's Novice.

Voltaic's three tiers, then the community scenario they were cut from - harder than Advanced, on a 42,007-entry board. psalmTS Voltaic is Voltaic S3's cut and sat at Expert above VT psalmTS Advanced, which S4 grades Advanced and snakbox additionally grades Hard. The S4 cut is the harder of the two on the only evidence there is, so it takes the Expert rung.
Voltaic S5's speed scenario, four tiers end to end.
The oldest switching lineage in the game, graded by target size across four cuts - jumbo, large, standard, small. One test at four difficulties with nothing else changing.
The same author's static cut, again sized rather than re-authored: jumbo, standard, small, extra small.
The goated dev lineage - easy, no-reload, no-reload static, then static small, which is the order its author cut them in.

Aimerz+'s static switching set, ordered by bot count and then by size: six bots slightly larger, five bots slightly larger, the standard week five cut, and that cut shrunk 30%. Its Novice rung was swapped down to an entry cut the sheets band Novice: the bottom of the ladder is meant to be a scenario a beginner can load without being beaten by it, and the difficulty there now comes from the threshold rather than from the test.
rungs: aimerz+ Static Switching 5 Bot Slightly Larger

Evasive Switching.$why: Switching between targets that are themselves moving and dodging. The thinnest of the five rebuilt categories at six families: 16 lineages carry two solid rungs and only six reach four. Four of the six close on a Voltaic Elite board under 1,500 entries, which is the honest ceiling of what anybody has measured this sub-skill on.

families.why: Voltaic's evasive ladder, four tiers, opening at 177,146 entries.
Targets that drift rather than strafe, so the switch lands on something still moving. Four Voltaic tiers.
Targets that reverse on contact, the sharpest direction change in the sub-skill. Four Voltaic tiers; the Elite board carries 645.
Evasive movement on no fixed pattern, so the switch cannot be pre-aimed. Four Voltaic tiers; the Elite board carries 367 and is the thinnest rung in the whole pool.
The smooth cut of tam's switching lineage, which asks for a controlled switch rather than a flicked one. Four cuts by one author, on boards from 4,255 to 138,805.
Four cuts of one scenario, sized and sped: easier, easy, standard, hard.
